headline: North Dakota orders hemp THC products off shelves by 11 December
dek: North Dakota said on 24 November that hemp products above the new federal 0.4 mg per-container THC cap must leave shelves by 11 December.
key_points: The North Dakota Department of Agriculture told retailers on 24 November to remove hemp products above the new federal THC limit before 11 December.
The federal cap is 0.4 milligrams of THC per container; North Dakota now allows up to 5 milligrams per serving, so one legal serving today is 12.5 times the coming federal limit.
The department said the state cannot keep hemp standards looser than federal law, and over-limit sales end unless Congress acts first.
North Dakota joins Maine, Vermont, Rhode Island and Iowa in telling businesses how to handle the 11 December change.
body: North Dakota has told hemp retailers to clear their shelves of intoxicating products before the federal hemp definition changes on 11 December. In an announcement issued on 24 November, the state Department of Agriculture said retailers must remove hemp products that exceed the new federal THC limit before that date, The Marijuana Herald reported.

The department's reasoning is simple: North Dakota cannot keep hemp rules that are less strict than federal law. Unless Congress steps in before 11 December, the announcement said, retailers cannot keep selling products above the federal line.

From 11 December, a finished hemp product with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per container falls outside the federal definition of hemp and is treated as marijuana. North Dakota currently allows up to 5 milligrams of THC per serving. On our arithmetic, a single serving that is legal in the state today carries 12.5 times the THC the federal rule will allow in an entire package.

That gap is why the order reaches so far. According to the Herald, the federal change is expected to remove most intoxicating hemp products, including THC drinks and edibles, and many full-spectrum CBD products that contain small amounts of naturally occurring THC. A typical multi-serving package of gummies or a pack of drinks would exceed the cap many times over.
> North Dakota is not choosing a hemp policy. It is telling retailers that, from 11 December, the federal line is the state line.

The change comes from a federal spending bill signed by President Trump in November 2025 that narrowed the legal definition of hemp. The restrictions were first set to apply on 12 November. Legislation signed on 2 September moved most of them to 11 December, while a first step banning cannabinoids the plant cannot make naturally took effect on 12 November, as we reported at the time.

Under the new definition, federal hemp is measured by total THC, including THCA, at 0.3% or less on a dry-weight basis, and the 0.4 milligram cap applies to finished products. The same 11 December date is also the deadline for Congress to pass government funding, which is why the fight over hemp has moved into the stopgap bill.

North Dakota's approach is the most direct version of a choice every state now faces. Maine's cannabis and alcohol regulators told businesses on 17 November to review inventory and take legal advice about existing stock. Vermont said it intends to write rules for an in-state market for products that meet Vermont limits but fall outside the federal definition. Rhode Island ordered businesses to transfer, destroy or quarantine non-compliant stock and to file quarantine records by 4 December. Iowa officials said earlier this month that over-limit products would come off the state's approved product list, according to the Herald.

North Dakota has taken neither Vermont's route of planning an in-state market nor Massachusetts' route of studying options; its regulator has simply aligned with the federal rule. North Dakota has a medical cannabis programme but no legal adult-use market, according to our North Dakota legal hub, which leaves no licensed channel for higher-strength THC products once hemp versions disappear.

Congress still has room to change the outcome, and both sides are pressing. The White House has asked lawmakers to protect non-intoxicating full-spectrum CBD in the stopgap spending bill, as we reported on 24 November. Fourteen Republican senators, led by Ted Budd of North Carolina, wrote to President Trump asking him to let the change take effect on schedule and to reject any federal framework for intoxicating hemp, as we reported on 25 November.

For North Dakota gas stations, smoke shops and convenience stores that stock hemp drinks and gummies, the practical deadline is now. Stock already on shelves may have to be returned, destroyed or written off. Suppliers selling into the state face the loss of a market unless they reformulate below 0.4 milligrams per container, a level well below a typical single serving.

Full-spectrum CBD makers are the group to watch. If Congress adopts the White House request, some of their products could be saved; if not, many will fall out of the legal market alongside intoxicating products, in North Dakota and nationwide.

Watch Congress and the stopgap funding bill, due by 11 December, for any change to the hemp definition or a CBD carve-out. Watch for more state agencies issuing North Dakota-style removal notices in the next two weeks, and for any guidance from the North Dakota department on how retailers should dispose of over-limit stock.
